meta.title: Who really said "I am too intelligent, too demanding, and too resourceful for anyone to be able to take charge of me entirely"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuinely Simone de Beauvoir — from her student diary, the Cahiers de jeunesse (1926–1930), not The Second Sex. The French original: 'trop intelligente, trop exigeante et trop riche.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1908–1986 · French existentialist philosopher, novelist & feminist theorist
answer.sourceLine: These are Beauvoir’s own words, written in her student diary — the Cahiers de jeunesse, 1926–1930. The French original reads ‘Je suis trop intelligente, trop exigeante et trop riche pour que personne puisse se charger de moi entièrement… Je n’ai que moi,’ and the popular English ‘too resourceful’ renders her ‘trop riche.’ The genuine attribution is often wrongly sourced to The Second Sex.

source.excerpt: I am too intelligent, too demanding, and too resourceful for anyone to be able to take charge of me entirely. No one knows me or loves me completely. I have only myself.
trail: The line is authentic Beauvoir: the French original appears among quotations from her diary Cahiers de jeunesse, 1926–1930 ↗.
The full French passage ↗ is credited to that same student diary, ending ‘Je n’ai que moi.’

The diary was published in French by Gallimard (2008); the shown English is an uncredited popular translation of the French ‘trop riche’ original, not a verified published rendering. A scholarly English edition covers only the early notebooks — Diary of a Philosophy Student ↗, Vols. 1–2 (1926–29), trans. Barbara Klaw — and is not confirmed to contain this entry.
source.excerptNote: French original: “Je suis trop intelligente, trop exigeante et trop riche pour que personne puisse se charger de moi entièrement. Personne ne me connaît ni ne m’aime tout entière. Je n’ai que moi…”
source.rightsHolder: Éditions Gallimard and the Estate of Simone de Beauvoir (Sylvie Le Bon de Beauvoir); English translation © University of Illinois Press
source.rightsNote: Although Beauvoir wrote these lines as a student between 1926 and 1930, the diary was first published only in 2008 (Gallimard, Cahiers de jeunesse), and the English translation dates from 2006 onward — so both the French text and its translation are firmly in copyright, held by Gallimard/the Beauvoir estate and the University of Illinois Press respectively.

author.name: Simone de Beauvoir
author.heading: About the author
author.bio: Simone de Beauvoir (1908–1986) was a French existentialist philosopher and writer, best known for The Second Sex (1949), a founding text of modern feminism. Long before that, as a philosophy student at the Sorbonne in the late 1920s, she kept intimate diaries wrestling with independence, solitude and self-worth — the notebooks published posthumously as Cahiers de jeunesse. This line comes from those youthful pages.

misattribution.heading: Genuine — but often mis-sourced
misattribution.intro: The words really are Beauvoir’s, so this is not a fabrication. The recurring error is about where they come from: they are pinned to her famous feminist works rather than to the youthful diary that actually contains them.

items.why: Aggregators and listicles routinely file the line among quotations from The Second Sex, but it predates that treatise by roughly two decades and appears in her student diary, the Cahiers de jeunesse ↗.
Most reposts (Goodreads, quote parks, Pinterest) give only the author’s name with no citation — e.g. this quotepark entry ↗ lists no book, letter or date.

misattribution.truthLine: The passage comes from Beauvoir’s Cahiers de jeunesse, 1926–1930 ↗, her Sorbonne-era diary, published by Gallimard in 2008 and translated into English as Diary of a Philosophy Student.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: Written when Beauvoir was a philosophy student in her late teens and early twenties, the passage is a private declaration of self-sufficiency: too rich in inner life to be wholly possessed by anyone, resolved to live knowing ‘no one will help me to live.’ It reads as an early sketch of the fiercely independent thinker she became.

Because the sentiment fits her later feminism so neatly, the line is frequently swept up into lists of quotations from The Second Sex — but it predates that book by two decades and belongs to the diaries, not the treatise.
detailsBody: The French ‘trop riche’ (literally ‘too rich’) is usually Englished as ‘too resourceful,’ and ‘se charger de moi’ as ‘take charge of me’ — both reasonable renderings, which is why the widely shared English text is a genuine translation rather than a fabrication.
